entities.name: European Council
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The European Council — established informally in 1974 at the initiative of French President Valéry Giscard d'Estaing and West German Chancellor Helmut Schmidt, and formalized by the Lisbon Treaty in 2009 as one of the EU's seven institutions with its own permanent President — is the body of the European Union's heads of state and government that sets the EU's political agenda, defines its general direction, and makes the highest-level decisions that shape the integration of Europe's 27 member states and approximately 450 million citizens.

The European Council is often confused with the Council of the EU (the Council of Ministers), the Council of Europe (a separate non-EU pan-European organization), and the European Parliament. It is distinct from all: the European Council consists of the EU's national leaders (presidents and prime ministers), meets several times per year in Brussels, and decides by consensus on the EU's strategic direction — from Brexit negotiations to COVID recovery funds to Ukraine support — making it the body where the highest political will is formed or blocked.

The European Council's decisions shape the fundamental course of European integration: the Maastricht Treaty's decision to create the Euro, the enlargement decisions adding new member states, the Lisbon Treaty's reforms, the response to the 2008 financial crisis (austerity vs. solidarity), the 2015 refugee crisis response, the Brexit negotiations with the UK, and the unprecedented COVID-19 recovery fund (€750 billion) all emerged from European Council summits. The permanent President role (Herman Van Rompuy, Donald Tusk, Charles Michel) has given the institution a more sustained voice in European and global diplomacy.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The European Council — the summit of European leaders setting the EU's political agenda for 450 million citizens, deciding the Euro, enlargement, and COVID recovery — is historically significant as the highest political institution of the world's most ambitious supranational governance experiment.
